blocks.x: Song Song Good evening and welcome once again to Jazz Review, a program of music and opinion. Brought to you by Custom Audio, the home of Stereoland at 7210 Washington Avenue. Now here's the man with the opinions, Doug Ramsey.
Thank you very much, Al. Good evening, everyone. Tonight, during the 50th anniversary year of Monk Hazel and Jazz, we're going to talk with Monk about his career. Please stay with us.
You know, 10 hours, I was running more like the Hawkins and Eddie Miller and Freeman School, you know.
We're just discussing John Coltrane with Monk Hazel, who has been in jazz since, what was the first year you played professionally?
Well, let's see, I was 8 years old. I was 11. That would be 1911. 1911? 1911.
Did they call it jazz then?

Yes. The name of the band that I played with, Doug, is funny. It was called Fishers Ragtime Military Jazz Band. Fishers? My father, my father was a drummer, bass drummer in the band. In those days, they used two drums. My father was the bass drummer, and a fellow by the name of Rag Baby Stevens was the snare drummer. And my father built a harness for me so that I could carry the snare drum. And we made this Rex Parade, which was the big carnival parade even then. And Fishers Band was the only band in the parade that played jazz. All the rest of them played march music and things like that. Who was Fish? Fisher. Fisher. F-I-S-C-H-E-R. Johnny Fisher. He had a band way back. And he had, you might know of some, heard of some of the Brunus boys, some of the Brunus boys. And Arshiel Barkay, he's George Barkay's brother. He was a clarinetist. And instead of using the B-flat clarinet, in parades, he always used the E-flat clarinet, which was much more piercing and high as thrilling. And people would, you could hear people holler, here comes Fisher's band from two, three blocks away because they could hear that clarinet well up in the air.
E-flat clarinet's pretty well disappeared these days.
Yes, they don't use them anymore anymore. Special.
Well, you must have been, what, seven or eight years old at this time?
We used to sing at that time.
And you carried a bass drum. No, a snare drum. A snare drum.

We used two snare drums. And another thing that we did, that they did in Fisher's band, like when the band was stopped and wasn't playing, most of the other bands would just play brr-r-rump, brr-r-rump, brr-r-rump, brr-rump, brr-rump, you see. Well, this rag bear, that's why they call him rag bear. And he, we worked some little things up between us, between he and I and my dad. And we brr-rump, brr-rump, you jazz like, you know, licks, like the kids do now in the high school and the college bands, you know.
Was that the first time, to your knowledge, that anybody had made those renovations?

Well, I don't know, Papa Lee, but he didn't play. You see, he wasn't union. He was non-union at that time. And he didn't play in the Rex Parade. The Rex Parade was the only parade that used a union band, and always did, you see. But I think Papa Lane played jazz in the parades that he played. But I don't know whether they did that thing with the drum thing, like we did, you know, played the jazz.
Back in those days, did your father and the other people who were playing that kind of music think of themselves as jazz musicians, as doing something different?

Oh, yes, because they were the only band, they and Jack Lane were the only two bands in town at that time that was doing that, you see. And that's why the name, the Ragtime Military Jazz Band, because they'd play anything. They'd play parades. They'd play funerals, weddings, anything like that. And then they'd play these all-day picnics where they would play jazz. But the instrumentation in those days was much different, Doug, than it is now. There were no saxophones. In those days, a band usually consisted of ten men. There'd be two trumpets, two trombones, maybe a baritone, two clarinets, and a bass, and the two drums.
Would it have sounded anything like, say, the Olympia or the Onward sound of the day?

No, no. Not like that. No, no, nothing like that. Because they used to play, they'd play a six-hour job. A picnic would last six in the evenings or twelve at night, or all day. They'd have all-day picnics. But besides jazz, they'd play things like Tiger Egg and those kind of things. But besides that, they played pretty, real pretty music. They played a lot of waltzes, because in those days, every third dance was a waltz. And they played mazurkas, shardishes, things like that. Most of them were pretty good musicians, contrary to what a lot of people make you try to believe.
Now, when you played something like a mazurka or a shardish, was there any improvisation involved in the solos?

No, no. You just played those straight? They read, they're just straight. And where did the jazz come in? That's where the improvisation came in, when they played the jazz tunes. Uh-huh. And they did, uh, what, they wouldn't only play things like the Tiger Egg and, and, uh, Panama, which was called number one, number two in those days. Uh-huh. And things like that, high society, they played. But, uh, uh, they would take the popular tunes of the day and turn them around. And, uh, one of the favorite things they used to do, they'd play a waltz. You see, and then maybe play four or five choruses of waltz. And then the drummers, the two drummers would make a turn, or what you call a turn around. And they'd, uh, pick the tempo up and enter a jazz tempo. And then they'd swing that same waltz, like Let Me Call You Sweetheart was one of them. They used to do that with, you know. Double the tempo or something? Yeah. Yeah, I used to, at one time I worked in a music store here, and the colored cellars, there used to be, when the orchestrations first started coming out, they used to have what they'd call doubles. It'd be walls on one side, and on the other side, they'd be written, arranged in a font structure, you see. And all the colored cellars would come in and want to know if I had any doubles, you know.
Did the Negro and white musicians play together?

Oh, yes, yes, yes. Not, uh, not, not, not as being high, Doug. You must understand this. We sat in, I sat in with them, I made records with them. You see, uh, uh, uh, uh, other than, uh, the, the, the belief is, New Orleans, as you know, has never been strictly segregated. There's never been no, no, just one town, one part of town where the colored people live. You can't go all, uh, outside of a few, few places like Lakeview or the real, I tell them what you call, well, you won't find Negro. But you can go right up St. Charles Avenue and go over one block or two blocks. And, and, and almost every neighborhood where I have lived in, since I lived in New Orleans, we've had Negro families in our block. Although, most of the times they were professional people like the barbers, things like that. They were real nice people. And, uh, when anybody was sick, they were the first people that would come.
Was there a substantial, uh, was there a substantial difference between the kind of music the, uh, the white jazz bands were playing and the, and the Negro jazz bands were playing?

Yes. It, it, it, uh, it was the same, uh, same kind of music, Doug. Uh, but the, the, the, the white fellas cleaned it up a little bit. It, it, it was just like the, the, the, the bands, the parade bands of nowadays.
Mm-hmm.
How do you mean clean it up? It was a little rough.
What was, what was there to clean it?
You mean they took the rough edges off? They took the rough edges out of it. And, uh, the, the, the, the tones, they played more in tune and things like that.
But the spirit.

It was, the spirit was the same. You, there's no white man in the world will ever capture the rhythm. A lot of us, a lot of us have come close, but there's no white man in the world will ever capture. Because that, Mr. Big gives you that. And he gave it to them.
Do you remember Jelly Roll Morton?

Yes, I do. Did you ever play with him? No, I never did. But I remember Jelly real well. I mean, more in New York than here. Mm-hmm. Because I was, I, I was in New York from, from, uh, 28 to 31. And that was just about the, the latter part of Jelly Roll Morton. Who'd you play with when, when you were there in those years? I was Joe. I worked with Jack Trettis. And I worked with a band, uh, in the Pennsylvania Hotel. Glenn Miller, we didn't have any brass. It was a, it was a takeoff on, on Rudy's valet. But we had, uh, instead of having, we had four saxophones, the trombone, and I doubled on the cornet. So I played all jazz. And, and we had three siddles and viola and, and four rhythm.
Dance band.

Yeah. Did Glenn Miller play any jazz at that time? Oh, yeah. Glenn played a lot of jazz. Uh-huh. Glenn played some things with, uh, with the, he made some records with the Mount City Booblowers. I remember that. And quite a bit with, with, with Condon when they first came to New York. And with, uh, with Nichols.
What was Glenn Miller's, uh, what was Glenn Miller's, uh, aspiration at that time? Did he want to continue to be a jazz trombone player? Did he want to write even in those days?

He liked to, he liked to write more than anything. I'm going to tell you something that maybe you might not know. But Glenn Miller has built more bands, more jazz bands, than any man in the country. The first band he built was Ben Pollack's band, in which Benny Goodman was at the time, Jimmy Mac Paul and all those kind of guys. The next band he built was, uh, was Ray Noble's band when he came over here from England, which was the best band in the country at the time. Uh, he built the Claude Thornhill's, I think, first band. Well, I know, and any number of bands, before he ever had a band of his own. Uh, and, uh, he came to New Orleans when that band was three weeks old. And, uh, they had broken in Boston, they had broken the band in. You mean his own band? His own band. It was the band, the only band he ever had. And, uh, they, uh, they came here to the Blue Room. They had broken the band in for three weeks in Boston. And, uh, I got Fazola for him. He didn't have a jazz clarinet player. And I got Fazola. Fazola was in New York working with, uh, uh, Wyman. Uh, I can't think of it. Not Abe Lyman, but the other. Not, uh, not, uh, not Lyman. Uh, oh, Arnheim. Gus Arnheim.
Oh, yeah.

And it was a bad band, and Foss didn't like it, but he was making Arnett the Quarter Week, which was good money in those days. So, Glenn and I called him from the Roosevelt, and Glenn could only afford $90, you see. So he told me, he said, Faz, I can only pay you $90 now, but this is, this band's going to be a good band. So Faz quit. Arnheim had come down here and joined Glenn, and he wanted me to go with him on drums. But I was making more money than that around here, because at the time I was on the staff band at, uh, WSMB. And, uh, I was, I don't know if that's a dirty word. No, no, that's, that's all right.
That's a good word.

And, uh, uh, and I was working at the 500 Club then. Leon Prima had the 500 Club then. That was before their revival, you know. Yes. You had to, you had to really scuffle around and start to try to hear any jazz. As a matter of fact, for a good while, we had, you know, we were playing the only jazz in New Orleans, because the rest of the bands would either go on Latin or go on arrangements and things that you couldn't hear in the real jazz. Yeah, those were tough days for traditional music, weren't they? And we only, we only played it in between shows. The show was the big thing. We had the Catgirl and the Christine and things like that and do about 10, 11 shows a night. And we'd probably play three tunes in between. And I played it, the clarinet, you know, with the drums, Leon would, Leon would just play the show.

Well, Monk, we want to get back to this. I want to have you back again in a week or so, so that we can play some of your older records, which I couldn't get a hold of right now. But let's take a short break here, and then we'll come back with some more modern music that I want you to kind of evaluate for us, if you would. We'll be right back after this message.

Our guest tonight is Monk Hazel, who is celebrating his 50th year in jazz as a drummer, melophonist, trombone, cornet, what else? You didn't get around to any of this, huh? How has jazz drumming changed since you began, Monk?

Well, it's changed all, it's changed, it's a different thing altogether. And that, Cooper is the one who started all that. Because, you see, when we started, we were taught that the drums were supposed to be felt and not heard. And the most you ever took was a two or a four bar break. A solo, you know what you call a solo, they call them solos now. There was never no drum solos like you have today. Because if you didn't come up and did that, they'd run you off the stand. But Cooper came into New York. And it's a funny thing, Doug, he played in the show, with red knickers called Rain and Shine, you see. And I spent $6.60 for a ticket to go hear this band. And then this band had old Miller and Miller and all, everybody who was big in those days was in this pit band, you see. And they did a big overture in which they played big band jazz. And Cooper must have had nine cymbals hung up there. And he did these paradiddles and all like they do. Now, all those things come out the method book, you see. And he did that. And I got so mad, I'd have to pay him about $6.60 to hear that, that I walked out on it. And then later on, he played at a place called the Hollywood Restaurant with Red. And I went in, I met Gene. And I told him, I said, you know what you're doing? You, you're ruining every kid in the United States. Because every kid in the United States is going to want to do what you're doing. And that's exactly the way it turned out. And then after him came David Tuff, Buddy Rich, and all those kind of fellas. And it's a different kind. You don't think, you don't think it's wrong. All we, all we had was maybe three basic beats. You had what they called a press roll,
you know,

and then you had a tid and ink on the top of the cymbal. And then the ride outs for the year, for the last choruses, which we all got off the Negroes, because that's the way they used to play. But you, if you didn't have a good press roll, well, you didn't get a job.
But you didn't think solos belong then.

How do you feel about it now? I still don't like them. I still, I tell you, you have to do them. But I never did go. I'll take four bars, or maybe eight bars. But no, no, no chorus or choruses. Or anything like that. Because I still don't think it did. It's not a, it's not a, it's not a, an instrument for a solo. It's not a melodia. You can't get any melody out of it. Although I've heard some boys do some wonderful things. Pete Fountain had a boy here. I first heard him with Tex Banerke. And he's the only one who ever completely satisfied me, because when he took a solo, he told a story. But these fellas, these fellas don't tell any story. And, and time, and that don't mean to think to them. I had a little, what's good, I had a little boy around here, by the name of, Paul Ferreira, who had pretty, he worked with Hertz for a while. He had pretty good hands, and pretty good feet. He used two bass drums at one time. And, uh, Buddy Rich was, uh, I was with Sharky at the time, at the Dream Room, and we were doubling with Buddy Rich. And, uh, Buddy and I got to talking, and I, I said, did you hear this kid cross the street with Hertz? And he said, no. I said, well, I want, I want you, I want to hear your opinion of him. Well, I had gotten Paul, before he went with Hertz, I had gotten Paul to, to thim it down, get away from all that noise. And he was getting, and so he was playing real good band drums. And, uh, orchestra drums. And it took me three months to do that, and then Al, he gets a job with, uh, two nights a week at the show bar here with Al, from three in the morning, till six in the morning, and Al broke down in two nights, where it took me three months to build, with the solo business, you know.

Monk, I want to get back, and we'll talk some more about, uh, drumming and, and jazz in, in general, but, uh, let's listen to, to one record, and I want to get your evaluation of it. stuff like stuff The End The End The End The End Okay, that was Charleston, of course. It's a band that Bob Thiel put together in New York to kind of spoof, I guess, old-time...

That's the way most of the hotel bands in the old days, especially the West Coast bands and the New York bands played. Chicago mostly, they always had a little... They never put in a little jazz in there through the Dixieland, and there was a trumpet and clarinet and trombone. I was surprised when you told me who it was that was on there.
Yeah, Jimmy McPartland was the trumpet player. It was sounding good.

Yeah, Pee-wee, Pee-wee's nose, really, really russling the mind. Is he? Yeah, Pee-wee, when I first went to New York, he was doing a lot of recording with Nichols and those guys. Yeah, yeah. And then the other time, he and Bix were living together.
Pee-wee, Russell and Bix?

Yeah, Pee-wee, Russell and Bix were living together. Must have been quite a household. At the 44th Street Hotel in New York, and they had a little yacht, you used to call them yacht pianos in those days. Really, two and a half octave piano. So they'd get, I used to go there around 11 o'clock. I lived on 53rd and Broadway. And I used to go there around 11, 12 o'clock, and they'd get up about that time, you know. And they'd have to sit the gin sitting on the bed table, you know, and they'd get up, and they'd go in the bathroom. And Bix would try, they'd take a swallowing, you know. And most of the time, the first one wouldn't stay down, and Pee-wee tried, and he couldn't stay, get it to stay down. Well, they'd keep trying until they got one to stay down. The minute they got one to stay down, they'd throw the whole bottle down, you know. That must have been bad gin. Yeah, and then Bix would sit down there, but oh, he'd play beautiful piano. He'd made a lot of things, you know, like that.
In a Mist.

In a Mist, and all those kind of things. And he'd sit down and play those. And Pee-wee, Pee-wee has played some wonderful things. Pee-wee, but at one time, he'd play erratic, and another time, he'd play real pretty, and another time, he'd do what Muggsy used to call squawk. Muggsy made a novel one time. And then one tune on there, he'd call it Pee-wee Squawks again. But Pee-wee was, well, he was here for quite a while with Lurie Primer, you know. They went ahead to that place over on Bourbon Street. That's a place called the Shim Shim. Oh, that's back in the early 30s, Doug. And Pee-wee was around here for about six months. And that's before Lurie got big, you see, before he got real big.
Pee-wee Russell has never been a conventional player.

No, no, he's never been, not only a conventional player, he's never been a conventional liver. He's tried to commit suicide four or five times. Has he? Yeah. Jumped in the ocean, Atlantic City. I think he jumped off about an eight or ten-story building in New York. Never did kill himself, though.
Next time you come down, I want to play you a...
He lived the way he plays.

Next time you come down, I want to play you a record that he and Red Allen made together just before Red died with a rhythm section of young guys in their 20s, very modern players. Yeah. And it's interesting how well it worked. Because both of them were so unconventional that they had harmonic ideas that fit in with what the young modern players were doing.
Yeah.

When we came on, you and I were discussing John Coltrane, and we never really got into that, so the people could hear your opinion of Coltrane in particular and modern jazz saxophone playing in general.

Well, he does some things. I haven't had a chance to dig him very much because he... And then that poor guy gets to die. I imagine he must have been quite young. Forty years old. Oh, he was that... I didn't think he was that old.
Yeah, just very...

But I just started hearing about him in the last five or six years. Before that, it was Bird and Hawkins and then a lot of those other guys like that. Prez and all those. I was very much familiar with him, but I wasn't very familiar with Coltrane. The fact is, I don't think I'd heard him more than once or twice until I heard your show. And then I listened to the whole show. I said, well, I want to find out what this guy does. And I listened to the whole show. And some things he did real nice, and some things he was a little far out.
Well, some of the earlier things he did, as you heard, were very melodic, lyrical.

Later, he got more frenzied as he got into another kind of music. Well, you changed like that. I've seen bands do that. I've seen bands make a national reputation playing one style. And the minute they get in the money, they changed the band around and play all together different. And it synced. Kenton is one that did that. He got more wild and more wild as he was. There's a funny thing about Kenton. I was out in California in 1934 to 1938 with Gene Austin. And I went down to Balboa Beach. And there had a bunch of boys in a band down there. A fella by the name of Hank Halstead had the band down there. And a bunch of the boys had been in a band called Ray Millers that he had left stranded here. He played at the Roosevelt. And he left them stranded here. And four or five of the boys, Vito Musa was one of them. Sammy Taylor was the drummer. He wound up with Phil Harris. And four or five of them. A fella by the name of Charlie DuPont and I kind of helped them out a little bit until they could get some money from California to get back home, you know. And they invited me to come down to Balboa and hear the band. And they were playing in a big ballroom. So they get this big, great big band, maybe 18 men. And Kenton's playing piano in this band, you see. And then a few years later on, he gets this progressive band. And he comes in the family store one night. And I got to talk to him. And I'd ask him, I said, now what I want to know is this. I've been listening to all this artistry and rhythm and all this business that you put in on. But what I want to know is every time it gets to time for you to play, you play like Father Hines. How come you do that? And he did.
What did he say?
He just left. He said, well.
That's very true.
He changed the way I play.
That's right.

And I don't think he ever changed. The last time I heard the band, he was still playing like Father Hines. Because that was his idol. Father Hines in those days was his idol, you know. And I thought that's so funny. He's got all this progressive music around. I think at that time he had Ferguson and all that bunch of guys. Rosalini and all that. Paul Desmond, I think, at the time, was with him too. Cooper. Bunch of guys. That's Shelley Mann. Every time it comes to... What do you think of Shelley Mann? I like Shelley very much. I like the things he's doing. He's way over my head. I didn't study much. stuff

to read with a piano player and I never did study with a drummer so I never got out of the Dixie landfill and didn't want to I played with some big bands in you know when I was younger but not in that vein

Hazel is our guest tonight on jazz review for those of you who may not know although if you live in New Orleans I don't see how that's possible mr. Hazel has been in jazz music 50 years this year as a drummer trombonist cornetist and also playing the mellophone mr. Hazel we're talking about Coltrane and his former drummer Elvin Jones is now on his own recording with his own groups I'd like to play you one one recording from Elvin's latest album and ask you to comment on it here it is 된된 The End
The End The End The End The End The End
The End The End The End

It reminds me of the way I look at this progressive music all the way. This is the third change that I've seen. The first was, some people like to call it ragtime, and then came what they used to laughingly call the pure jazz.
Some people still do.

Some people still do. And then it got a little bit more progressive and a little bit bop came in then. And that didn't go, the people didn't buy that at all because they couldn't understand it. Most of the public I'm talking about. It had a lot of musicians, it had a lot of the musicians, it had an impact on some of them. And I tell you, the first time I heard Dizzy in person, we had been to Toronto and we had a night off in Chicago coming back home. And so Julian Lane, who had a lot of the way to do it. And so Julian Lane, who was a trombone player, and I was walking up and down State Street and we see this sign up here, there's a Gillespie, you see. So I'd heard a few of his records. So I said, let's go in. So we went in and he was walking behind the ball like Sharky. He used to walk on the ball playing the seats here. And we sat down and bought a drink, $2.55 for a drink. So he had six men, I think. He had the cornet, clarinet, drums, piano. And the guy on played the barring, sax and fives. So they're playing for about 20 minutes and I'm trying to find out what they're playing. I never have found out what they're playing. So the guy who was playing the barring, and the vibes, he's looking at me and he's digging us. So finally, after about 20 minutes, he puts the vibes down and picks up the saxophone. And he plays eight bars of How High the Moon, you know, and I'll let thank you.
Oh, yeah. He knew you were in trouble.

That was my introduction to Dizzy. But then I got to know him a little later. We were working at Roundtable in New York and Tyree Glenn had the band that was alternating with us. And Dizzy and he used to, Dizzy would come in there and they would talk a lot. Dizzy had a little round ass, like a potent type. No, not a beret. No, this is like a potent type where he's in the shrine. And he was going to go over to some little country over in Africa. And he was going to be the prime minister over there. Like Louis wanted Louis to come over there and be the king. So this was going to be. Tyree's telling me all this. He said he's going to be the prime minister of this country. He told me the name of the country. I don't remember.
It didn't work out, though, apparently.
No, it didn't. He never did go.
Well, Dizzy's an interesting man.
Yeah. Well, any of those guys. We had the characters in our age, too. Bix was quite a character.
Yeah. Did you know Bix well?

Yeah, I knew Bix pretty well. Like I tell you, Moore threw that. And then he came down a couple of times when he was with Whiteman. He and Frank Trombauer were with Whiteman. We like broke the thing up. They did a concert, you see. And there was no jazz at all. So after the intermission, we were in the alley side. It was old St. Charles said up there. They've torn it down now, I think. Well, I was delegated to go up and speak to Whiteman and tell him that we wanted to hear some Bix and Tram, you see. So I walked up to him and I told him, and I must have said it in a gangster-like way or something. And he looks at me and he says, well, I'll tell you, all we're going to do when we go back, we're going to play Metropolis and American in Paris. And Trombauer's going to do it in the shoes. You know, these great big long shoes that the clowns and the circuses just get up on the top of those things and walk around. That was in the act. So I told him, I said, now we've got to have some of Bix and Tram or we're going to break this thing up. Like I say, he must have taken me for a gangster. So when they go back in, they get the band all on the stage and everything. He comes out to the footlights and he says, ladies and gentlemen, he says, I have had a lot of requests and a lot of threats for Bix and Tram. And he turns around and he tells them, you're on your own. He walks off stage, you see. So Roy Bog was a piano player, one of the piano players at that time. So he started vamping, singing the blues, you see. So they played that and then they played about three or four things and broke up the house. But if we hadn't have done that, we wouldn't have got one note of jazz out of the whole thing.
